    According to recent reports, ace left-hander Tarik Skubal, winner of the last two American League Cy Young awards and far and away the top free agent of the 2026-27 class, has agreed to terms with the Upcoming York Mets on a nine-year contract worth $450 million, reports the New York Post. The deal has a $45 million signing bonus with no options or opt-outs, per SNY, as well as a full no-trade clause, so the Mets have locked Skubal up for the full nine years. Further, there are only $30 million in deferrals, according to the New York Post. The deal is pending a physical.

    Once finalized, the deal will make Skubal the highest-paid pitcher in Major League Baseball history, in terms of both total contract value and average annual salary.

    Skubal, who turned 30 years of age on Nov. 20, is the No. 1 ranked talent on our list of the top 50 free agents for this offseason. Here's part of Mike Axisa's write-up:.

    "Excluding Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who was a special case as a Japanese star with no MLB track record, Skubal is the best starting pitcher to hit free agency since Gerrit Cole in 2019. He revealed few long-lasting effects from the NanoScope elbow surgery in May and remains a capital-A Ace with terrific surface stats and under-the-hood performance indicators. Skubal brings four swing-and-miss pitches to the table (four-seamer, changeup, slider, curveball), a near MLB-best ability to limit exit velocity, and elite strike-throwing ability (MLB's third-lowest walk rate since 2023). Build an ace starter in a lab and he would look a lot like Skubal. He'll play the entire 2027 season at age 30, and given the things teams can do with pitchers these days, Skubal figures to remain a frontline starter for most of a long-term contract. He's the only true balance-of-power player available in free agency this offseason. Skubal can swing a division race and a postseason series all by himself.".

    Sources indicate that over the last three seasons, Skubal has pitched to a 2.42 ERA and an FIP of 2.48 in 546 innings spread over 88 starts. That amounts to a total WAR of 17.7 since the start of the 2024 campaign. Skubal remains foremost in the discussion for best pitcher in baseball, and this signing reflects that reality.

    Since Skubal was traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers from the Detroit Tigers leading up to the 2026 deadline, he was ineligible to receive the qualifying offer from the Dodgers. As such, the Mets will not be penalized a draft pick for signing Skubal.

    The nine years here aren't record-setting, as the longest pitcher contract remains the 12-year deal that Yoshinobu Yamamoto signed with the Dodgers. Yamamoto's $325 million was previously the largest contract for a pitcher -- obviously excepting Shohei Ohtani, as he's a two-way player -- so Skubal's $450 million shatters that record.

    Sources indicate that coming off a disappointing 88-loss campaign in 2026, the Mets, major-spending owner Steve Cohen, and lead decision-maker David Stearns needed to make an offseason splash to improve their chances of a 2027 rebound and inspire a perhaps disaffected fan base. Skubal more than qualifies. He'll front a Mets rotation that also includes 25-year-old right-hander Nolan McLean, who himself has frontline long-term potential. In Queens, Skubal joins a roster that also includes the All-Star likes of Juan Soto, Francisco Lindor, and Bo Bichette.

    In a recent development, further, the Mets just locked up young outfielder A.J. Ewing to an eight-year, $95 million extension and we all know plenty about Soto's monster contract. The Mets now have Soto through 2039, Skubal through 2035, Ewing through 2034 and Lindor through 2031.

    The rotation for the Mets right now looks something like:.

    Given the large outlay for Skubal here, the Mets should be all-in on improving the ballclub for the 2027 season, which means we shouldn't expect them to stop with just signing Skubal. That last spot in the rotation, as such, should be ticketed to someone else outside the organization at present, whether a free agent or a trade acquisition.

    The landing of the top free agent available no doubt ramps up the pressure on Stearns and the Mets to deliver a playoff berth and a deep October run in 2027, but Skubal's presence also makes it much likely that such a feat comes to pass.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • A solid start was masked by an overly passive 5-4-1 and ultimately ended in a 5-1 defeat for Dino Toppmöller and Eintracht Frankfurt.
    • According to recent reports, after three winless games, Eintracht Frankfurt faced Liverpool on Wednesday evening.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 25.10.2025 in den Kategorien Champions League mit 0 Kommentaren.

    A solid start was masked by an overly passive 5-4-1 and ultimately ended in a 5-1 defeat for Dino Toppmöller and Eintracht Frankfurt.

    According to recent reports, after three winless games, Eintracht Frankfurt faced Liverpool on Wednesday evening. Dino Toppmöller lined up in a 3-4-3 formation. Zetterer started in goal after extended discussions in the media. Amenda and Theate took up the half-back positions, while Koch operated as the central center-back. On the flanks, Kristensen and Brown were deployed. In midfield, Götze and Larsson formed the double-eight, with Doan and Bahoya on the wings and Knauff starting as the central striker.

    The visitors from Liverpool arrived in Frankfurt with a similar situation: four consecutive defeats, including losses to underdogs like Crystal Palace and Istanbul. Arne Slot lined up in a 4-4-2 formation. Mamardashvili started in goal, with Konaté and van Dijk forming the central defense. On the flanks, Frimpong and Robertson defended, while Jones and Szoboszlai operated in central midfield as number eights. Gakpo and Wirtz occupied the wings, and up front, Isak and Ekitike formed the striking duo.

    According to recent reports, after the game, Markus Krösche mentioned: “In the end, it’s about showing a completely different level of aggressiveness in the duels.” A topic that has been omnipresent around Frankfurt for weeks—and came into the spotlight again against Liverpool. But why did Frankfurt struggle so much to even engage in the duels?

    Sources indicate that this is a translated analysis. You can find the original here: https://spielverlagerung.de/2025/10/24/die-sache-mit-der-passivitaet-mx/.

    Liverpool with Incompact Number Eights.

    According to recent reports, from the home side’s perspective, the game initially unfolded differently than the overall narrative suggested: it started off stable. In the first ten minutes, Dino Toppmöller’s side largely operated from a 3-4-3 structure in their higher build-up, with particular focus on the half-backs Theate and Amenda. Liverpool’s two forwards in the 4-4-2 mid-block struggled to gain access to the half-backs positioned in the half-spaces due to their narrow starting positions.

    Recent findings suggest that this repeatedly created horizontal pressing angles—i.e., side approaches—which carried a high risk of being dribbled past. Theate, in particular, was able to exploit this thanks to his very vertical first touch. Consequently, Liverpool’s number eights, especially Szoboszlai on Theate’s side, were often forced to move from the center into the half-space to press the advancing half-back. This opened central spaces next to them, into which Frankfurt’s number eights could advance and increasingly become available as passing options.

    Hugo Larsson, in particular, was able to receive the ball from Theate multiple times, as the right number eight—Götze, or sometimes Doan and Knauff when positioned deeper—tied up Jones in Liverpool’s right half-space. This created, in the opening minutes, large pockets of space between Liverpool’s central number eights, allowing Larsson to push forward relatively freely.

    Frankfurt Finds Larsson in the Center.

    This initially meant that Liverpool struggled to immediately disrupt Frankfurt’s build-up after the half-backs carried the ball forward. Often, the visitors responded by having Jones instinctively step out onto Larsson. However, due to the long pressing distance from the half-space into the center, he usually arrived late in the duel, allowing Larsson to hold onto the ball with his composure and often stabilize play via a relieving pass back to Theate. Jones stepping out also forced Gakpo, the far-side winger, to move into the half-space, reducing his ability to provide width for potential switches. Frankfurt, however, made too little direct use of these far-side spaces in the opening phase.

    Larsson’s Focus on Breaking Free.

    Sources indicate that despite dropping deeper, Larsson’s focus was also on another problematic area in Liverpool’s pressing: the space between the first and second lines. The narrow positioning of the two forwards is meant to isolate passing lanes from Frankfurt’s first build-up line into the defensive midfielder. In practice, though, their adjustment to players dropping behind them—beyond their tight starting positions—was limited.

    Larsson frequently found pockets in the blind spot between the two forwards and became available through central center-back Koch in the defensive midfield zone. Szoboszlai and Jones were often tied up in the half-spaces by the inward-running Bahoya or Kristensen, and the gaps between Liverpool’s first and second pressing lines were relatively wide, preventing them from intuitively stepping out onto Larsson.

    Against the forwards’ rearward pressing, the Swede was able to turn effectively and drive into the center with the ball. In some cases, this movement primarily served to draw Liverpool’s double-striker formation together, thereby giving the half-backs more space for diagonal dribbles—here, Larsson often simply laid the ball off. At other times, he actively sought progression and diagonal switches to advancing players in wide areas, most often targeting Brown on the left flank, which proved fairly effective in the opening phase.

    However, Wirtz’s active rearward pressing limited space for Bahoya in the deep left half-space, meaning left-back Frimpong didn’t need to step out. As a result, Brown was frequently isolated on the wing, repeatedly facing 1v1 situations, which he struggled to handle consistently.

    Liverpool Reveals Spaces Both Wide and Centrally.

    Speaking of Bahoya: He frequently looked to make diagonal runs into the space behind Szoboszlai to get into the center and be vertically available for Larsson. However, Larsson struggled noticeably in these situations to find Bahoya in the right spaces. On one hand, this was because during his diagonal dribbles he focused heavily on the flank, sometimes neglecting scanning toward the center. On the other hand, this orientation also exacerbated Brown’s isolation on the left wing: with Bahoya positioned centrally, there were often few nearby support options, while Theate rarely pushed up consistently in these moments. As a result, Brown was frequently isolated in 1v1 situations without passing options.

    Too Fragmented or Well-Focused?

    As Brown became increasingly involved in Frankfurt’s play, a newly introduced dynamic emerged: Wirtz pressed closer and more directly onto Brown, which opened up the vertical passing lane from Theate in the half-space to Bahoya, who repeatedly offered dropping movements.

    At this point, one could discuss whether Liverpool’s pressing appeared too fragmented: on the one hand, the number eights were oriented too man-focused (see above), creating central spaces that were potentially exploitable. On the other hand, Wirtz’s wider positioning and Szoboszlai’s lack of compensatory movement meant these spaces were actively playable for Frankfurt. Or not?

    Sources indicate that on the other hand, it must be noted: what appears fragmented can also be well-prepared or intentional. While Bahoya was technically available as a passing option, Liverpool reacted very effectively in these situations. Right-back Frimpong tracked his dropping movements directly and consistently, while Wirtz and Szoboszlai stepped up, creating situations in the half-space where Bahoya faced 1v2 or even 1v3 disadvantages, simultaneously closing potential lateral passing options. Considering that Bahoya is primarily a player who looks to provide vertical depth rather than withstand direct pressure, this approach made sense: Brown was pressed more directly, Theate was forced into the half-space, and Bahoya came under immediate pressure, often leaving him with only the option of a backward pass.

    Wirtz’s more direct stepping up also addressed an concern from the opening minutes. Frankfurt’s narrow starting positions had allowed Brown to remain available laterally to Theate, creating a very horizontal pressing angle. This enabled Brown to open up vertically and play deeper to Bahoya or carry the ball himself—something that ideally should have been prevented.

    Recent findings suggest that after Frankfurt’s relatively stable start—facilitated by higher initial possession that gradually decreased due to enforced verticality—Liverpool increasingly found their rhythm. This was mainly because Frankfurt allowed it. The Eagles set up in a 5-4-1 deep block, prioritizing blocking rather than actively pressing. This was particularly evident with striker Knauff: he lightly tracked Liverpool’s half-space dribbles but rarely contested the duels actively. Consequently, there was no isolation on lateral passes from the first pressing line, allowing Liverpool to shift play between the center-backs and repeatedly dribble forward. Frankfurt’s midfield was forced into constant lateral shifts, which repeatedly opened spaces within the 5-4-1 block.

    Liverpool thus created excellent conditions to exploit gaps inside Frankfurt’s 5-4-1 structure. Both number eights, Jones and Szoboszlai, occasionally broke forward ahead of Frankfurt’s second pressing line, acting as part of the first build-up line between center-backs and half-backs (or “wing backs”), creating temporary 5-0-5/3-2-5 spacing. The intent was twofold: first, technically strong players like Szoboszlai and Jones could dribble and exploit small diagonal spaces; second, the expansive build-up created direct backward passing options via central center-back van Dijk, enabling quicker lateral switches and further straining Frankfurt’s shifting.

    Sources indicate that the main aim, however, was to position as many players as possible around the block—both in front and behind—to force Frankfurt’s number eights to step out reactively onto Liverpool’s dribblers in the half-space, while simultaneously opening “blind-spot” spaces in front of the defensive line. Structurally, this was facilitated on the right by Konaté, who could push Szoboszlai wider from the half-right position. This, in turn, pulled Frankfurt’s left winger Bahoya slightly out of compactness (likely to prevent a 2v1 in width behind him), while Larsson was forced into more active blocking—slightly stepping up without actively contesting duels, creating minimal defensive shadow. As a result of these positional adjustments, spaces often emerged between Bahoya and Larsson, which Florian Wirtz sought diagonally.

    Liverpool Seeks Ways Around the Block.

    According to recent reports, this created some interesting patterns in the lay-off play. Ekitiké occasionally moved into the number 10 zone, positioning himself horizontally to the right following Wirtz’s diagonal runs, allowing Wirtz to lay the ball off to him. Since Wirtz immediately stepped back into the “play & move” rhythm, these pressure situations occasionally opened opportunities for direct forward progression into deeper areas—even if they were not fully exploited in the opening phase.

    It also became apparent that a defensive focus on blocking inherently involves some degree of reactivity. Drops from the last line were not actively tracked but responded to reactively. The priority was securing depth first and defending only upon receiving passes. This approach gave Wirtz and Ekitiké additional freedom in the half-space—players of their quality can exploit such pockets effectively. This was particularly noticeable in the first-touch lay-off patterns.

    Because Liverpool could switch the ball with ease, it was increasingly played from one wing-back to another. Personnel shifts were very dynamic: Jones, Wirtz, or Szoboszlai occasionally operated wide as wing-backs, while Konaté and Robertson advanced into the half-spaces. Switches could be executed directly through the half-space movements of van Dijk. The core issue for Frankfurt lay in the 5-4-1 block: ball-far wingers and full-backs tended to drift too far into the half-space. After Liverpool’s switches, these players moved relatively uncontrollably back into width to track their direct opponents.

    At this point, the question arises as to why Frankfurt focused so heavily on blocking and, after deliberately allowing switches, responded in such a fragmented way by pushing out wide.

    Recent findings suggest that this repeatedly created pockets of space between full-back and half-back that Frankfurt’s 5-4-1 block was supposed to prevent, but Ekitiké consistently sought and exploited them between Theate and Brown. The matter was compounded by the fact that, although Frankfurt tended to push out, the long pressing distance in width made it difficult to prevent Liverpool from seeking 1v1 situations. Brown was repeatedly placed under intense pressure in these duels, as diagonal pressing in a deep block is one of the most complex tasks: he needed to both close depth to block dribbles and runs from the half-space and defend the flank. Early on, however, Brown managed this reasonably well, and a subsequent ball win from him led to Frankfurt’s opening goal.

    Frankfurt’s wide players increasingly dropped back during Liverpool possession to support the full-backs in loose numerical superiority pressing. Yet, Doan on the right frequently failed to isolate the backward passing lane, often losing track of Jones and Robertson, allowing Gakpo to break free and enable another switch. On the left, the rotational setup was less dynamic, but Gakpo was slightly more proactive than Frimpong (later Bradley) in taking on Kristensen directly in 1v1s. Initially, however, there was insufficient depth support, leaving Gakpo relatively isolated. Kristensen’s effective blocking of crossing options further limited the Dutchman’s effectiveness in these situations.

    Higher wing-backs as the Key Point.

    According to recent reports, after conceding, Liverpool pushed further forward, particularly in how their wing/full-back (depending on Szoboszlai’s temporary role in the back three) and number eights operated higher. Robertson and Jones increasingly formed a pair on the left side, while Gakpo moved more centrally in response to his earlier isolated position. Robertson pushed up as the left wing-back to free himself from Doan’s pressure and, together with Jones, create a 2v1 against Kristensen. This allowed Gakpo to repeatedly hint at depth in the half-space or actively position himself in the box—crucial since crosses had previously been only partially effective.

    The width pair also allowed Doan to drop more frequently and shift from the half-space into wider positions, reopening spaces in the ball-side half-space. These were exploited primarily by Wirtz when diagonally dropping, forming a kind of dynamic trio with rotating coverage of width and half-space alongside Gakpo and Robertson. Typically, Wirtz, as the trigger for Phase 1 dynamics, dropped diagonally into the half-space and laid off to Robertson moving forward, while Jones pushed diagonally into the half-space center behind Wirtz, later being targeted by Robertson as the receiving player.

    Recent findings suggest that the center. This splitting of the back five deliberately opened up deep half-space channels behind Frankfurt’s defensive line. At the same time, the Reds often sought to occupy the ball-far full-back and half-back, creating central spaces. Isak exploited these spaces with diagonal runs, using his pace advantage over Theate effectively.

    When these spaces couldn’t be played directly, Liverpool remained in motion. One of Liverpool’s key strengths is maintaining this dynamic play through constant rotation of width. For example, Wirtz moved wide when the deep ball didn’t arrive, seeking 1v1 situations against Kristensen. The Frankfurt defender struggled against the German, who consistently cut inside. Through these inverted dribbles, Wirtz repeatedly found half-space areas—often connecting with Jones or Gakpo, who were probing the space in front of the defensive line. Frankfurt’s defenders continued to struggle with decisions between stepping out and securing depth.

    Recent findings suggest that it also became clear that the wing-backs increasingly made overlapping runs when the wingers had the ball. For full-back Kristensen, this meant he no longer consistently engaged directly with the winger, often leaving the duel to Doan to track the ball, while he dealt with the overlapping runner. Consequently, Frankfurt’s lateral dueling became more passive, giving the winger more space and time on the ball. Simultaneously, channels opened centrally in front of the defensive line because Kristensen was occupied by the overlapping full-back and Doan’s wide diagonal drop failed to fully isolate the passing lane to the center. This allowed Liverpool increasingly comfortable ball circulation on the wings with central connection options, opening opportunities for shots from the edge of the box—especially for the number eights, who could join centrally and occasionally shoot from distance.

    This increasingly prominent Liverpool dynamic, combined with Frankfurt’s continued failure to isolate backward passes, forced Frankfurt in the middle of the first half to operate deeper in their 5-4-1 block, constantly defending in a low posture. The original blueprint—to lure Liverpool out, provoke errors into the compact block, and then attack their rest defense on the counter—became progressively more difficult to execute.

    This was largely because Frankfurt’s wide players, Bahoya and Doan, were increasingly drawn into defensive duties and had to drop deep, meaning they couldn’t provide the vertical width after winning the ball that they typically should as deep runners. At the same time, Liverpool tracked any vertical movements from Frankfurt’s wide players very effectively through their wing-backs; on the ball-far side (here Bradley), they aimed to anticipate the advance of the far-side winger and mark him with the far-side wing-back, making it difficult for him to break free.

    Additionally, Liverpool used their deeper number eight—usually Szoboszlai—and van Dijk to double up on the ball-near attacker Knauff in the half-space, preventing him from being played into effectively, which worked well: Knauff struggled to hold the ball for wall passes after turnovers. Konaté covered any spaces behind this double, particularly for second balls. However, the underlying problem remained that blocking implicitly assumes winning the ball within the defensive line when defending deep. After ball recoveries, Frankfurt could hardly progress from the back against Liverpool’s immediate numerical overload, which instantly triggered overloading counter-pressing and closed off vertical passing options to the number eights—the weak point in Liverpool’s rest defense system. As a result, Frankfurt’s defenders were often forced into long balls under pressure.

    Recent findings suggest that in other words, even after going 1-0 down, Frankfurt continued to lose possession. Because they operated deeper, these turnovers occurred in more advanced positions of Liverpool’s pressing, creating direct pressure and limiting structured buildup. The space that needed to be covered on counters was larger than in the mid-block early in the game.

    It has been revealed that one could also discuss how a counter-attacking approach correlates with pressing and collective compactness. Frankfurt occasionally pressed individually and fragmentedly in response to certain cues (e.g., second dribbles in the half-space or wide distances), but lacked a clear, collective transition from the block into pressing. This allowed Liverpool to face minimal pressure in their first build-up line and develop their dynamic play, effectively freezing Frankfurt into passive blocking.

    Andrzejewski et al. (2022), in Analysis of team success based on match technical and running performance in a professional soccer league, analyzed over 600 Bundesliga games across two seasons and correlated various performance indicators with team success. One key point: more duels won correlated with more counterattacks. Similarly, Lepschy et al. (2021) found in analyses of the 2014 and 2018 World Cups that teams with higher duel success and effective counters were more successful. These findings suggest that both the quality and quantity of duels are linearly linked to successful counterattacking.

    According to recent reports, at the same time, Liverpool created relatively few chances from open play. They generated five major chances, with two goals from set-pieces and one counter leading to a 3-1 halftime lead. Their main struggles were in finishing crosses and chance creation around the box. A side effect of their play around Frankfurt’s block was that much creative personnel was positioned wide, limiting their effectiveness in tight spaces. Players like Wirtz and Jones rotated around the block with the wide players, sometimes causing problems in small-sided scenarios inside Frankfurt’s compactness. These options were therefore missing in key areas.

    It has been revealed that build-up should not be judged solely by whether it leads to goals but also by how it shifts game momentum. This increasingly shifted in Liverpool’s favor, largely due to their adjusted progressive play.

    After two corner goals just before halftime—each exploiting target players (van Dijk and Konaté) to find the “blind spot” created by horizontal movements of blockers like Ekitiké and Robertson—little else occurred in the first half. Liverpool continued to control the game against Frankfurt’s deep block, increasingly using direct diagonal switches to the far side to give their wide players more time 1v1 against Frankfurt’s ball-far full-backs or to create depth in the box.

    These passes were occasionally imprecise, causing “ping-pong” situations in front of Frankfurt’s box around the central number eights. Liverpool faced minor counter-pressing problems but could usually manage them with collective back-pressing and tactical fouls.

    At halftime, Arne Slot brought on Chiesa for Isak, and Liverpool increasingly adopted a clear back-three setup in a 3-5-2 with slight adjustments. Wing-backs Robertson and Bradley operated deeper in their starting positions, intending to pull Frankfurt’s full-backs wider and open half-space channels for the inside wingers Wirtz and Gakpo. Diagonal breaking movements—acting as connectors between wing-back and number eight—remained visible, particularly Wirtz on the right. During ball possession, he would pull Konaté out, quickly lay off to Bradley, and then exploit the space between Brown and Theate while moving in the “play & go” rhythm.

    Overall, Eintracht also struggled in the second half to consistently track or cover the drops from their last line in front of the second block. This repeatedly created 2v1 overload situations for Liverpool in width. Theate occasionally pushed out slightly but could not exert meaningful pressure on Wirtz. Instead, he often opened spaces in behind, which Chiesa repeatedly exploited to be played directly in behind—often from passes by Konaté.

    Direct diagonal balls to advancing wing-backs became more common, with these players benefiting from slightly deeper starting positions to gain a dynamic advantage over Frankfurt’s wide defenders (Brown in particular struggled against Bradley), allowing these balls to reach deep positions. The persistent matter, however, remained that Frankfurt struggled to get into the box.

    Sources indicate that frankfurt offered very little themselves. Apart from isolated actions following ball recoveries that couldn’t be converted directly into counterattacks, little developed. Even during brief periods of higher possession, the team remained vulnerable to Liverpool counters. This was primarily because Frankfurt’s number eights continued to operate high, leaving the space in front of the first-second line rest defense largely uncovered. Fast attackers—especially Ekitiké—and the dribble-capable Chiesa consistently exploited these half-space channels in Liverpool’s secondary attacks.

    Sources indicate that the 4-1 goal came from a Liverpool turnover after Szoboszlai freed himself in the number eight zone with a dribble. Wirtz received the ball deep in the half-space between Brown and Theate. Gakpo drove forward from the space in front of Frankfurt’s number eights to the far post, exploiting the goalkeeper’s “blind spot,” and finished. (The goalkeeper’s blind spot is often an underestimated reference point for attackers.) The 5-1 was a long-range shot from Szoboszlai following a horizontal lay-off from the wide area into the half-space. Such lay-offs occurred frequently throughout the game but had rarely been finished consistently.

    Overall, it was an interesting game—predictable in some ways but also grinding at times. Frankfurt must significantly improve their defensive activity and pressing to get back on track in the coming weeks, particularly against top teams. Liverpool, on the other hand, secured notable morale-boosting points. The team revealed clear potential for improvement, but also remained prone to errors. Overall, it was a favorable game for Slot and Liverpool.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With the majority of Week 11 in the books, the NFL playoff picture is beginning to take shape. While several teams remain in the thick of the postseason race, others are already looking ahead to the offseason and the opportunity to improve their rosters through the 2027 NFL Draft. Where does each team currently stand in the first-round draft order, and which positions could they look to address? Those answers and more can be found below.

    As a reminder, five teams -- Green Bay, Indianapolis, Jacksonville, Chicago and the Los Angeles Rams -- do not own a first-round pick in 2027 due to trades, including the Micah Parsons, Sauce Gardner, Jeffery Simmons, Jordan Davis and Myles Garrett deals.

    #141875. Timberwolves, Grizzlies reportedly hope to move to Eastern Conference after expansion; who makes more sense?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1457 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

    Timberwolves, Grizzlies reportedly hope to move to Eastern Conference after expansion; who makes more sense?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1457 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The NBA is barreling toward expansion, and the addition of two latest teams would have enormous basketball implications for the remaining 30.
    • It has been revealed that several teams are eager to do so, according to The Athletic.
    • It has been revealed that getting out of the West would be appealing on several levels.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The NBA is barreling toward expansion, and the addition of two latest teams would have enormous basketball implications for the remaining 30. Perhaps the biggest is geographic. Both Seattle and Las Vegas are located firmly in the western half of the United States. Should those cities eventually be granted teams, they would play in the Western Conference, leaving the league with unbalanced conferences. Therefore, someone in the West would have to move to the East in order to balance the conferences at 16 teams apiece.

    It has been revealed that several teams are eager to do so, according to The Athletic. While the New Orleans Pelicans are not out of the running, the likeliest teams to move in realignment, for now, are reportedly the Minnesota Timberwolves and Memphis Grizzlies.

    It has been revealed that getting out of the West would be appealing on several levels. Of course, there are obvious basketball reasons for preferring the East. Putting aside the decades of Western Conference superiority that hold little weight in the long run, the two teams best positioned to succeed over the next decade or so are the San Antonio Spurs and Oklahoma City Thunder. As the Upcoming York Knicks learned last June, the easiest path to a championship is avoiding Victor Wembanyama and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander until they've already spent seven games battling each other.

    It has been revealed that but this isn't just a basketball conversation. The NBA, like most major American professional sports leagues, tilts east. There are simply more major cities in the Eastern half of the country than the Western half. Of the league's 30 existing teams, 17 play east of the Mississippi River: the 15 already in the Eastern Conference, along with the Timberwolves and Grizzlies.

    It has been revealed that travel is simply easier playing in the East. One projection of how many total miles each NBA team will travel this season has only the Miami Heat in the top half of the league, with the other 14 slots belonging to Western Conference teams. That projection has the Heat crossing 24 time zones, while every Western Conference team crosses at least 36.

    So Minnesota, Memphis and Fresh Orleans are all incentivized to move, and with the Grizzlies and Timberwolves seemingly favored, let's evaluate the cases for each.

    Sources indicate that the fundamental case for the Grizzlies is geographic. Memphis is further East than Minneapolis. As The Athletic points out, it is closer to more Eastern Conference teams as well, as it is within 600 miles of five East teams (Charlotte Hornets, Atlanta Hawks, Indiana Pacers, Chicago Bulls and Milwaukee Bucks). This not only makes travel easier for the Grizzlies, but for those teams as well.

    Recent findings suggest that while the Timberwolves are considered the better team right now, Memphis is probably the team better positioned to be competitive in the long run. Minnesota's best players -- Anthony Edwards, LaMelo Ball, Jaden McDaniels and Ayo Dosunmu -- are all in their mid-20s earning market-rate salaries, and Rudy Gobert is much older at 34. Plus, the Timberwolves are essentially devoid of first-round draft capital.

    Recent findings suggest that the Grizzlies have a significant draft surplus, and their best players -- Cameron Boozer, Cedric Coward and Zach Edey -- are still on their rookie deals. If the idea is balancing the two conferences competitively, even if the Timberwolves have a higher immediate upside, the Grizzlies are probably the team we should expect to contend longer.

    Industry observers note that and then there's the matter of maintaining established rivalries. While neither the Grizzlies nor the Timberwolves are franchises steeped in historical success, Minnesota's last few years have established the Timberwolves as genuine postseason rivals to several important Western Conference teams. They've faced Nikola Jokiċ and the Denver Nuggets in multiple recent playoff series. They've faced Luka Dončić in multiple recent playoff series, even if they've come against different teams. Their series against the Spurs last spring included a Wembanyama ejection.

    Industry observers note that the NBA may prefer to maximize the number of games Edwards plays against these high-profile opponents because there are existing narratives surrounding those matchups. In that case, keeping the Timberwolves in the West makes sense while allowing the Grizzlies to shift to the East.

    Minnesota's geographic case is a bit more nuanced. While Memphis is closer to more teams, Minnesota is closer to a few geographically convenient ones. If we assume for the moment that the latest, 16-team conferences are going to come with four divisions featuring four teams each, Minnesota's proximity to Milwaukee, Chicago and Indiana makes for an easy four-team pod.

    The rest of the conference becomes remarkably easy to group from there. We have three more roughly Midwestern teams (Cleveland, Toronto and Detroit), five in the Northeast (New York, Brooklyn, Boston, Philadelphia and Washington) and four in the Southeast (Charlotte, Miami, Orlando and Atlanta). Just move one of those Northeastern teams to the Midwestern group -- presumably Washington, as it doesn't play in the existing Atlantic Division -- and you're set. If the NBA wants to make divisions a more prominent part of scheduling moving forward, Minnesota makes doing so much easier.

    There's also the idea of giving Edwards, one of the league's more personable stars, an easier path to the NBA Finals by getting him away from Wembanyama and Gilgeous-Alexander. The NBA is, ultimately, a star business, and if stacking the deck in Edwards' favor helps build him up as one of the faces of the league, there is obvious appeal in doing so.

    It has been revealed that by all accounts, we are far closer to resolution on a Las Vegas team than to the return of the Sonics in Seattle. Bidding has seemingly been more robust in Las Vegas, and an announcement is expected in the near future. If an announcement on Vegas comes before one in Seattle, there will be a brief period in which the NBA has an odd number of planned franchises.

    Industry observers note that that does not mean that it will ever actually play a season with only 31 teams. Seattle, as commissioner Adam Silver has described, is much more of a turnkey operation than Las Vegas because of its arena situation and preexisting basketball history. In theory, a Seattle team could be revealed much later than a Las Vegas team and still begin play in the same season. For now, the reported target for expansion teams to tip off is the 2028-29 season. However, if Seattle's bidding process takes too long for the two to begin play at the same time, or worse, if no Seattle group manages to put forth an acceptable bid in the near future, the possibility of one or even multiple seasons with 31 teams rather than the expected 32 probably does exist.

    The NBA -- and every other major American professional sports league -- has had unbalanced conferences in the past. None do now. It creates scheduling headaches, and it's just blatantly unfair. Forcing some teams to overcome 15 opponents to reach the Finals while others only have to top 14 makes playing in the smaller conference too much of an advantage, and since the conference presently believed to be the superior one (the West) would be getting the Las Vegas team, competitive balance would go from a problem to an outright crisis.

    Fans have been calling for the abolition of conferences for decades now. Getting it to actually pass a vote would be harder. Realignment is voted on by the board of governors, so abolishing the conferences theoretically would be as well. Eastern Conference owners love having an easier path to the playoffs and the gate revenue those postseason games generate. This is where the idea of a season or two with just 31 teams in the league carries some appeal. It could give the NBA an opportunity to test the abolition of conferences provisionally with the idea that conferences would return when the league reaches 32 unless a newly introduced vote determines otherwise.

    Industry observers note that the appeal of removing conferences altogether stems from the inherent fairness of a playoff system determined solely by record. There have been concerns about how removing the geographic component of playoff scheduling would affect travel, but there are potential solutions there. Returning to the "2-3-2" home-court format would minimize travel, or higher seeds could be allowed to select opponents in the early rounds to decide for themselves how they'd like to prioritize travel. The odds are obviously against the removal of conferences altogether, but expansion offers a potential opportunity to test it without committing to it long-term, and that's an opportunity the NBA would be foolish not to at least explore.

    2026 NFL playoff picture, standings: 49ers reign over NFC, Jaguars slip in AFC, wild-card battles heat up

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that if there is any truth to the adage that the NFL season does not truly start until Thanksgiving, then now is the time to start taking the playoff race seriously.
    • Anyone that aims to lock up a first-round bye in the NFC has to get through the San Francisco 49ers, which is a daunting task considering how dominant they appeared on the Week 11 edition of "Sunday Night Football.".
    • Sources indicate that and in the AFC, the Jacksonville Jaguars learned a difficult lesson on Sunday about how slim the margins are in the race for the No.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that if there is any truth to the adage that the NFL season does not truly start until Thanksgiving, then now is the time to start taking the playoff race seriously. As the calendar turns to Week 12 and a loaded holiday slate, all seven seeds in both conferences are up for grabs, and there are a number of teams beyond the current cut line that could not only make their way into the bracket but also compete for home-field advantage in the postseason.

    Anyone that aims to lock up a first-round bye in the NFC has to get through the San Francisco 49ers, which is a daunting task considering how dominant they appeared on the Week 11 edition of "Sunday Night Football.".

    Sources indicate that and in the AFC, the Jacksonville Jaguars learned a difficult lesson on Sunday about how slim the margins are in the race for the No. 1 seed when they suffered a costly setback against the Newly introduced York Giants.

    With seven weeks of regular-season action to go, here is a snapshot of the playoff picture in both NFL conferences.

    Sources indicate that remaining schedule: vs. Chiefs, at Patriots, at Packers, vs. Bears, at Broncos, at Dolphins, vs. Jets.

    The only blemish on the Bills' resume is a three-point divisional loss to the Patriots, but that should not come back to bite them in the AFC East race as they hold a commanding four-game lead. It does make them vulnerable in the battle for the conference's No. 1 seed, though. The schedule is about to stiffen up following a four-game stretch in which Josh Allen feasted on beleaguered opponents and the defense corrected its early-season woes by allowing no more than 12 points in any of those contests.

    In a recent development, remaining schedule: at Steelers, vs. Dolphins, at Jets, at Raiders, vs. Bills, at Patriots, vs. Chargers.

    Industry observers note that that the Broncos fended off Fernando Mendoza and the Raiders was critical for Denver's chances of winning the AFC West. Sean Payton's squad holds a tiebreaker over the Chiefs thanks to their higher win percentage against common opponents. It was a rare win by double digits for a team that is prolific at squeaking out victories by a one-score margin and increased the win streak to six games, which is tied for the longest in the conference.

    Remaining schedule: at Commanders, vs. Saints, at Browns, vs. Chiefs, at Panthers, at Colts, vs. Ravens, vs. Browns.

    Regardless of what occurs on "Monday Night Football," the Bengals cannot slip out of line for a top-four seed. They stand a game and a half clear of the Browns and Steelers in the AFC North. As one of the hottest teams in the league, they take an offense that is seemingly unstoppable into the Week 11 finale against the Commanders.

    Remaining schedule: vs. Titans, at Bears, vs. Steelers, at Texans, at Cowboys, vs. Commanders, at Colts.

    Trevor Lawrence endured uncharacteristic struggles in a loss to the Giants that halted the Jaguars' momentum. In each of their previous four games, they scored at least 31 points. They managed only 18 against Fresh York. The AFC South is still theirs by a three-game margin, so the defeat only has implications for seeding inside the top four. This team went all-in at the trade deadline and would thus figure to be disappointed with anything less than the No. 1 seed, but so long as everything comes together in the postseason, one loss in Week 11 will not haunt them.

    Remaining schedule: at Bills, at Rams, at Bengals, vs. Patriots, vs. 49ers, at Chargers, vs. Raiders.

    The battle with the Broncos to secure home-field advantage in the Wild Card round could come down to the last week of the season. The Chiefs have done nearly everything they can to lock up one of those prized seeds yet find themselves on the outside looking in due to Denver's tiebreaker in the division. Kansas City has been mauling overmatched opponents of late and needs that to translate to the much stiffer competition that lies ahead over the next five weeks.

    Sources indicate that remaining schedule: vs. Raiders, vs. Bengals, vs. Falcons, at Giants, at Ravens, vs. Colts, at Bengals.

    The Browns hold a tiebreaker over the Steelers for the No. 6 seed because of their divisional win percentage. They split the regular-season series with Pittsburgh and won their only other AFC North contest, 13-10, over the Baltimore Ravens. Among the more pleasant surprises of the entire NFL season is what first-year coach Todd Monken continues to achieve in turning Deshaun Watson back into a serviceable starting quarterback and how defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg constructed a competitive group following the offseason Myles Garrett trade.

    Sources indicate that remaining schedule: vs. Broncos, vs. Texans, at Jaguars, vs. Ravens, vs. Panthers, at Titans, at Ravens.

    It was only three weeks ago that the Steelers held sole possession of the AFC North lead. Everything since then has been a disaster. They no-indicated a week ago in a primetime loss to the Bengals and, on Sunday, were on the wrong side of the Eagles, who snapped a seven-game losing streak. That in-state loss marked a new low for the 2026 Steelers. They remain on the right side of the postseason cut line, but it is a tenuous position.

    Recent findings suggest that no team outside the top seven is better than 5-5, and that lone .500 team will be without its quarterback until further notice. The Patriots (5-5) would be the top contender to move up the ladder if Drake Maye were healthy, but in his absence, the door is open for teams a little further down. That includes the Texans (4-6), who could become just the second team in NFL history to start a season 0-4 and reach the playoffs. The pickings are slim behind them, as the Ravens (4-7) and Raiders (4-7) are operating with a backup quarterback and rookie signal-caller, respectively.

    Remaining schedule: vs. Seahawks, at Giants, vs. Rams, at Chargers, at Chiefs, vs. Eagles, at Cardinals.

    In a recent development, if a decisive win over a fellow championship contender and a 35-point outburst against the NFL's top defense does not cement the 49ers as Super Bowl favorites, then nothing will. San Francisco is undoubtedly the team to beat. Mike Evans' return in the Mexico City Game injected even more life into the offense and gives Kyle Shanahan yet another weapon to deploy in the weeks to come as he unleashes an unstoppable attack on the rest of the league. The NFC is the 49ers' to lose.

    Sources indicate that remaining schedule: vs. Bears, at Falcons, vs. Titans, at Vikings, vs. Giants, at Bears, at Packers.

    In a recent development, the Lions hold a tiebreaker over the Bears for the NFC North lead with the greater win percentage in division games, but that will not matter in just a few days when the head-to-head result between the two on Thanksgiving determines who has the inside track to home-field advantage in the Wild Card round. Detroit, as it stands, is the top threat to the 49ers at the top of the conference and owns the kind of offensive star power it would take to unseat them from the NFC's catbird seat should they square off in the postseason.

    Industry observers note that remaining schedule: at Colts, vs. 49ers, at Seahawks, vs. Browns, at Lions, at Cowboys, vs. Eagles.

    In a recent development, the Giants passed their biggest test of the year on Sunday when they took down the Jaguars in a colossal 23-18 victory. Every other win on their ledger is against a sub-.500 team, so the Week 11 triumph was by far the most impressive and legitimized their division lead. They remain the only NFC East team with a winning record and own a defense that seems capable of keeping them in control of their own destiny in the hunt for a top-four playoff seed.

    Remaining schedule: at Buccaneers, at Vikings, vs. Saints, vs. Bengals, at Steelers, vs. Seahawks, vs. Falcons.

    Such is the state of the NFC South that the Panthers are merely .500 yet own a two-game lead over the rest of the division. Every other team is 3-7. There exists a realistic path for Carolina to move up to the No. 3 seed since the NFC East is nearly as weak as their own division, but that is probably the ceiling. Back-to-back wins and Chuba Hubbard's emergence as a prominent bell-cow running back have the Panthers trending the right way.

    Recent findings suggest that remaining schedule: at Lions, vs. Jaguars, at Dolphins, at Bills, vs. Packers, at Lions, at Vikings.

    According to recent reports, the Jeffery Simmons effect is obvious. The Bears are unbeaten since they traded for the superstar defensive tackle, and he came through with three sacks on Sunday to match a career high and aid Chicago in defeating the Saints, 21-13. Simmons' presence will be of the utmost importance next week against the Lions' incredible rushing attack and the following week when the Bears take on Jacksonville in an intra-conference blockbuster.

    In a recent development, remaining schedule: vs. Falcons, vs. Panthers, at Patriots, vs. Lions, vs. Commanders, at Jets, vs. Bears.

    In a recent development, is it time to be concerned about the Vikings? All of a sudden, Minnesota has lost three of its last four games. Sure, the "Sunday Night Football" disaster can be chalked up to playing against a stellar offense in a not-even-remotely-neutral environment in Mexico City. But the Vikings are going to have to beat teams of the 49ers' caliber to get to the mountaintop, and they have done nothing but lose to them over the last month. The elite defense will only take them so far, and on days like Sunday when not even that group demonstrates up, things can get really bleak.

    Remaining schedule: at Rams, at Saints, vs. Bills, vs. Dolphins, at Bears, vs. Texans, vs. Lions.

    In a recent development, the NFC North is what most expected the NFC West to be in that it could send three or four teams to the postseason. There is a battle between the two divisions for the final wild card spot. The Seahawks and Rams are both 6-4, so Seattle holds the tiebreaker based on win percentage in division games. But the Packers then hold a tiebreaker over Seattle due to their conference win percentage.

    The NFC North and NFC West will cannibalize themselves to an extent, which may open the door for the Cowboys (5-6) to sneak their way into the No. 7 seed. But there is a chasm between Dallas and the teams ahead of it in terms of overall team quality. The Seahawks (6-4) and Rams (6-4) are both more complete squads. There might only be room for one of them to get into the bracket, though, which would be a surprise given the former's status as the reigning champion and the latter's preseason outlook as the Super Bowl favorite.

    The record has been scratched amid Aaron Rodgers' "Last Dance.".

    In a recent development, for the first half of the 2026 season, the Pittsburgh Steelers seemed well on their way to making it back to the postseason and giving Rodgers, who is playing in his final season in the NFL, one last kick at the can. The club entered its Week 9 bye at 6-2 on the season and riding a four-game winning streak. Upon their return to action, however, their season has gone sideways.

    Pittsburgh has now dropped two straight games, including a 19-16 defeat to the Joe Milton-led Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday. Whatever the issues that have led to this skid are, the Steelers need to get them corrected in a relatively quick fashion, as it's not hyperbole to say their season is teetering.

    It has been revealed that the Week 11 loss dropped them to 6-4 on the season and has them falling from the No. 6 seed down to the No. 7 seed. Despite being on the bye, the Cleveland Browns leapt over them thanks to a tiebreaker. After splitting the regular-season series, Cleveland at the moment possesses the tiebreaker over Pittsburgh due to its superior record within the AFC North (4-3 vs. 3-3).

    Industry observers note that on top of jockeying for position with the Browns, the Steelers now need to concern themselves with a few AFC teams just outside the current playoff picture. While their season has been turnt upside down following the fractured fibula to Drake Maye, the Patriots (5-5) are a game behind Pittsburgh and own the head-to-head tiebreaker thanks to a win back in Week 2.

    According to recent reports, speaking of tiebreakers, the Steelers' main competition for a wild card spot could end up being the surging Texans. Houston is 4-6 after Week 11, but has been lurking, especially as C.J. Stroud has been enjoying a career year under center. These two AFC clubs will square off in just a couple of weeks from Pittsburgh in Week 13.

    Before then, the Steelers will host the Denver Broncos, while the Houston Texans will host the Baltimore Ravens. At DraftKings Sportsbook, Pittsburgh is a 2.5-point underdog at home next week, and the Texans are a 6.5-point favorite. If those games go according to the spread, this Week 13 contest sets up Houston with an opportunity to move to 6-6 and gain the head-to-head tiebreaker with a win over the Steelers, who'd tumble down the standings and possibly out of the playoff picture entirely.

    Pittsburgh would then finish out the season with games against the Jaguars (road), Ravens (twice), Panthers, and Titans (road). While that's not a gauntlet, no game is guaranteed given the way the Steelers have been playing post-bye.

    Industry observers note that right now, Mike McCarthy's club sits at +138 to miss the playoffs. That feels like one of the best bets you can make in the futures market coming out of Week 11.

    How Game Balls work: Six are awarded to standout players from the slate of teams that won their contests, and only one player on a team can get a game ball.

    Recent findings suggest that carter was a man possessed in Upcoming York's win over the Jaguars. Coming into this game, the former first-round pick had two sacks on the season, and he ended up matching that total with two sacks on Trevor Lawrence on Sunday. Carter led the team with eight pressures and was a massive reason why the Jaguars offense was off-kilter for the bulk of the afternoon.

    Abdul Carter is taking over 😤JAXvsNYG on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/v6djuFIjYZ.

    In a recent development, simmons continues to pay dividends for the Bears after the Bears acquired him in a blockbuster trade with the Titans. The defensive lineman tallied three sacks in the win over the Saints. That gives Simmons five sacks since coming over to Chicago. He's just the third player in NFL history to have at least five sacks and three wins in his first three games with any franchise.

    This Jeffery Simmons guy is pretty good at football📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/jdGX4RdikK.

    Industry observers note that the Cowboys offense exploded for 51 points in a dominant win over the Titans. Prescott accounted for five touchdowns on the afternoon, the fourth time in his career he's notched at least five scores. He's also the fifth player in NFL history with multiple games of at least 300 yards passing, four passing touchdowns and one rushing touchdown in a career.

    6 drives6 TDsTHE COWBOYS' OFFENSE IS ELECTRICTENvsDAL on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/4FQeNa6kbk.

    Kelce turned back the clock in Kansas City's 34-7 win over the Cardinals. He was Patrick Mahomes' most targeted weapon in the winning effort and finished with a team-high 74 yards to go along with two touchdowns. Kelce is the fourth-oldest player with at least two touchdown receptions in a game in NFL history. Those scores also got him to 90 career touchdowns, which is the fourth-most by a tight end in NFL history.

    Kelce gets his second touchdown of the first half!AZvsKC on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/VOaPtsJiBo.

    Coleman would not be denied as the rookie back was the key cog of Denver's offense in the 38-24 win over the Raiders. He hit paydirt three times on Sunday and extended his touchdown streak to three-straight games. Coleman is the first Bronco with at least 100 yards rushing and three rushing touchdowns since Mike Anderson (2005 vs. Jets).

    Hat trick for Jonah Coleman ‼️LVvsDEN on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/FQNYZWdwKH.

    Recent findings suggest that purdy sliced up what has been the best defense in the NFL in the Vikings en route to a 35-10 win in Mexico City. Against Brian Flores' blitzes on Sunday night, Purdy completed 16 of his 18 pass attempts for 195 yards and two touchdowns, which resulted in a 148.8 passer rating. This performance could very well propel him atop the MVP odds and has San Francisco on a clear road to the No. 1 seed in the NFC.

    What a throw by Brock Purdy!MINvsSF on NBC/PeacockStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/EbcQmS99j1.

    On the one hand, Jameson Williams' 57-yard touchdown catch was worth celebrating. It broke open the game for Detroit en route to their win over the Buccaneers. That mentioned, a backflip probably wasn't the way to go, especially when the Lions are merely a week removed from Aidan Hutchinson suffering a season-ending ACL tear after celebrating a sack.

    Aidan Hutchinson had a season ending injury celebrating last week…So naturally his teammate Jameson Williams does this after scoring pic.twitter.com/aw490Oacbq.

    You could feel everyone in Detroit tense up as he leaped in the air.

    Justice Hill was about to add to Baltimore's lead in the early stages of the second quarter as the Ravens back ripped off what looked to be a 37-yard touchdown. However, just before crossing the goal line, Hill has the ball knocked free. It then flew through the back of the end zone for a touchback.

    Recent findings suggest that TD turns into a touchback! Panthers ball!BALvsCAR on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/qpWNoHVtvw.

    Hill would redeem himself with a touchdown run later in the quarter, but that was a killer in what proved to be a 35-33 defeat at the hands of the Panthers.

    Industry observers note that one of the wildest plays of the weekend came in Dallas where rookie wideout Carnell Tate wisely realized he was untouched on a short throw by Cam Ward. After making the catch, the Titans receiver quickly got up and ran 59 yards to the house for a touchdown. Upon review, no Cowboys defender touched him while he was on the ground, so it was a remarkable heads-up play by Tate.

    The awareness by Tate for the TD‼️📺: @NFLonFOX pic.twitter.com/iI11vKXeap.

    It has been revealed that the Steelers receiver was ejected from the Week 11 loss to the Eagles after poking the eye of Philadelphia defensive back Cooper DeJean. Metcalf already had one unsportsmanlike penalty to his name for the game, and that infraction then sent him packing in the third quarter. This was the third ejection of Metcalf's career.

    DK Metcalf has been ejected in PhillyCBS | Paramount+ pic.twitter.com/johlxzOD1J.

    Before his ejection, Metcalf caught just one of his four targets for 2 yards in what has been a forgetful season for the veteran pass catcher.

    Sources indicate that it was a head-scratching day from the officials in the Jaguars-Giants contest at MetLife Stadium. Specifically, there were two instances where replay seemed to get it wrong. On the first play of the second quarter, Jags running back Chris Rodriguez took a third-and-2 snap up the gut for what looked to be a first down. However, replay assist chimed in and relayed that the runner was short of the line to gain. Liam Coen disagreed, challenged, and ultimately won. Again, Coen needed to challenge a replay assist. As J.J. Watt noted on the broadcast, that's not how this is supposed to work.

    J.J. Watt: "This is not how replay assist is supposed to be used." 🏈🦓🎙️ pic.twitter.com/LIHKDa6Io9.

    In a recent development, later in the contest, Parker Washington appeared to make a fantastic touchdown catch. However, the officials on the field initially called it an incompletion, prompting Coen to throw the red challenge flag again. Unlike that prior attempt, however, Coen was unsuccessful. Despite Washington getting both feet in bounds, securing the ball and not bobbling it, the ruling on the field stood.

    "I did not think he lost possession of the football ... I think it's a touchdown fellas."@GeneSteratore disagrees with the call of INCOMPLETE after review pic.twitter.com/b2T3eoe5my.

    CBS Sports rules analyst Gene Steratore said later in the broadcast that he spoke to the NFL offices and they felt that there was not enough clear and obvious evidence to overturn the ruling on the field.
